Brain-Map Poster — Input Screens & Publish Workflow

The four source layers used to build the poster (full resolution, 2752×2064, for annotation), each with what the code does and which files are responsible — then the end-to-end publish flow.

1 Empty brain stencil assets/1-empty-stencil.png

The bare hand-drawn brain outline — gyri and sulci only, no content. This is the base canvas every other layer sits on top of, and it defines the coordinate space ("poster space") that all the marker boxes are measured in. You just hand it over as a brainimage.png — nothing happens to it yet.

2 Stencil with the icons assets/2-with-icons.png

The stencil with the hand-placed icons baked into the raster — this is the current poster master the engine actually consumes. Because the icons are pixels in the image, they can't carry their own links or tooltips; that behavior comes from the invisible marker layer (step 3).

Under the hood

poster-content.json names this file via "brain_image": "brain.png". The engine build_poster.py measures its aspect ratio with Pillow, scales it, base64-embeds it into the generated SVG/HTML, and reflows the README cards and connector curves around it. Swapping the art is just pointing brain_image at a new file and rebuilding.

FileRole
private repo / poster-content.jsonSingle source of truth; brain_image picks the art.
image-map-readme / build_poster.pyReads the art + content, emits svg / html / png / pdf.
3 Stencil with the purple blockouts (staging input) assets/3-staging-blockouts.png

While placing the icons, use an image editor that has a layering feature. I use Procreate. For each icon, I create a layer that is a clipping mask of the icon, which typically is a square. I fill that in with color that the code will recognize as a bounding box for a click location. Flattened to a single image and handed to the program (find_brain_links.py), it is a staging map that says “make these spots interactive” — the clickable / hover regions are marked visually, by painting, instead of by typing pixel coordinates. The program reads the boxes and figures out where each marker goes.

Under the hood

find_brain_links.py turns the painted boxes into coordinates. It walks the image pixel by pixel and classifies each as the marker colour (the committed is_blue() test keys on the royal-blue callouts), buckets the hits into a 40-pixel grid, and keeps only the dense cells. It then flood-fills neighbouring cells into connected components — one component per painted box — takes each component’s bounding rectangle, and converts it from native pixels into poster space using the brain’s placement constants (BRAIN_IMAGE_X / Y / WIDTH plus a scale factor). The result is printed as ready-to-paste boxes; you then add each one’s tooltip / href by hand, since only you know which icon a box belongs to. From there build_poster.py renders the boxes as the invisible hover / click zones layered over the flat art.

FileRole
private repo / staging imageHand-painted: one purple box per icon, each on its own layer, over the icon.
image-map-readme / find_brain_links.pyDetects the painted boxes, prints poster-space coordinates.
private repo / poster-content.jsonWhere the detected boxes land, under brain_markers (you add tooltip/href).
image-map-readme / build_poster.pyRenders each box as an invisible hover/click zone over the art.
4 Stencil with the ID numbers assets/4-id-numbers.png

The same marker boxes, outlined and numbered 1–N. It's the index map: each number ties a box on the art back to its entry in the marker list, so you can place and audit boxes without eyeballing a busy zoomed-out overlay.

Under the hood

verify_markers.py walks the brain_markers list in order (the numbers are the list indices), converts each poster-space box to native pixels, and writes a padded, red-outlined review crop per marker into verify/. It also runs automated checks (blue-label centroid for URL markers, ink coverage for icons) that can gate a build — but the per-number crop is the authoritative check you actually look at.

FileRole
image-map-readme / verify_markers.pyEnumerates + checks markers, writes numbered review crops.
private repo / verify/Per-marker crops, named by index (git-ignored output).
5 The publish workflow private repo → image-map-readme → roots.origamisoftware.com

How a content edit becomes the live, password-gated poster at roots.origamisoftware.com/me.

This all runs as a GitHub Workflow. You commit a file to the private repo and wait — there are no manual build or deploy steps. The change then shows up live, and the server brings the new version up with a blue-green deployment (the new build is staged beside the running one and swapped in, so there's no downtime).
  1. 1
    Start in the private repo
    The private repo holds the personal data: your README text, the brain art, and the passphrase gate. Committing a file here is the only manual step — everything after it is automatic.
  2. 2
    Check out the engine + the private repo
    The workflow checks out the engine repo image-map-readme (the shared build engine) alongside the private repo (your content and art). The engine is improved upstream and flows in here.
  3. 3
    Build the artifacts
    image-map-readme / build_poster.py reads private repo / poster-content.json + private repo / brainimage.png and emits spencer-brain-poster.svg / .html / .png / .pdf. The HTML is the self-contained, shareable file.
  4. 4
    Gate + publish
    private repo / deploy/make_gate.py AES-256-GCM encrypts the HTML behind the ME_PASSPHRASE riddle and commits it as me/index.html into the landing repo roots.origamisoftware.com.
  5. 5
    Go live (blue-green)
    roots.origamisoftware.com deploys onto the server with a blue-green swap — the new build is brought up beside the running one and switched in, so there's no downtime. nginx then serves the one static gated file at roots.origamisoftware.com/me. The visitor's answer decrypts the poster in-browser; the page only ever ships ciphertext.
